prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: Across the five frames, the bright lower band places the counter and items at roughly 0.2–0.8 m from the camera wearer, while the woman remains approximately 1–2 m away and the darker rear walls, doorway, and room interior lie farther behind her. She shifts from the right side of frames 1–2 toward the centre in frame 3, becomes partly cropped at the left edge in frame 4 as the viewpoint turns right, and returns on the right in frame 5; the changing scale suggests camera motion and turning more than a simple continuous approach or retreat. The map makes foreground–background separation, the counter’s reachability, and major occlusions clearer than RGB: the counter obscures lower bodies and the person blocks parts of the rear room, while the counter is within the camera wearer’s arm’s reach and appears within the woman’s reach in the later frames. Fine depth is unreliable around silhouettes, transparent or reflective surfaces, and small counter objects, and some walls appear implausibly bright or flattened, so metre estimates and distances between objects are only approximate.
descriptions.segmentation: The map consistently isolates one person, placing her about 1–2 m in front of the camera wearer: right-of-centre in frames 1–2, near centre in frame 3, partly cut off at the left edge in frame 4, and right-of-centre again in frame 5. Her mask grows and changes shape as the viewpoint closes or turns, showing that she occupies the near workspace behind the counter; no second person is segmented, and the only separately labelled object is a TV-like rectangular object in frame 4, positioned ahead and to the right of the cropped person. The silhouettes clarify which visible regions belong to the person despite blur and clutter, including partial occlusion by the counter and image boundaries, but they do not encode metric depth, facing direction, gaze, or whether objects are within reach without RGB/depth context. The map is unreliable as a full scene inventory because it omits the counter, bins, doorway, display equipment, and most small objects, and the TV label may be a misclassification of nearby equipment.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects one person but is sparse in frames 1–2, fuller in frames 3 and 5, and absent in frame 4; the detected body moves from right-of-centre to centre, then is lost when the person is largely cropped during the camera turn, before reappearing on the right. In frames 3 and 5 the upper-body skeleton is roughly upright behind the counter, with both magenta hand clusters low and forward near counter height, placing the hands approximately 1–2 m from the camera wearer and close to objects on the work surface; the counter itself is nearer, around 0.2–0.8 m. The head landmarks lie above the shoulders, but their noisy clustering and the lack of stable facial orientation do not support a reliable claim that the person looks toward the camera wearer; RGB suggests her head is generally angled downward or sideways rather than consistently front-facing. Pose reveals limb arrangement and hand proximity that motion blur and occlusion obscure in RGB, but missing joints, floating points, distorted arm geometry, lower-body occlusion, and the total frame-4 dropout make exact facing, reach, and inter-joint distances unreliable.
